She is not to leave the hospital before the other Sisters arrive. Even if the Mother House community were left without a guide by Sr. A. Adelaide's departure, she is not to worry. She should organize everything well and take the time needed. Advice and forecasts about the new work. She confides to her a plan of hers regarding transfers.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have just received your letter together with the one from the Bishop of Acqui; I cannot understand why you asked what to do about the Bishop, when I had written that I would do everything.1 Well, now everything is done; I have already assigned the Sisters and hope you will be pleased; but for charity's sake don't leave until they have arrived and you have put everything in order, because even if Sr. A. Adelaide had to come away, for the moment there would be nothing to fear; first you must think of leaving everything in good order.2

  2. Give my regards to Don Tito and tell him that as soon as I return from Rome I shall come to see the Ovada hospital; and the same to the President.3

  3. I urge thrift on you, for you know well how we stand, and you are right, my dear daughter, that our needs are great; alas, you cannot imagine how much is needed here, my God!

  4. I hear you have a girl at risk; God be blessed — if only girls at risk could also be placed in that Hospital.4

  5. Take care of yourself. All you have done, you have done well; I tell you just one thing: I want you never to separate, for pity's sake, especially certain ones like Sr. A. V... you understand me. With these you need fifty eyes.5

  6. I hope you will soon call the two religious; though they are still few, because with home nursing coming it is a serious matter if there are only 5 Religious; if only there could be at least 6.6 But enough, slowly, in time.

  7. When there are no seriously ill patients, it seems to me the night watch could be omitted, provided there were a bell, you know, as at Cento; that would do. So the Religious would rest and, if they had to go out, would be ready; so see whether it could be done.

  8. Now I think I shall thank the Bishop myself too. Now I'll confide something to you: here too we have to contend with Marchionesses.7 Patience.

  9. Pray and have others pray, for charity's sake, that the Lord may send me qualified teachers, for I need them; I am very much afraid that Adelaide, once here, would not be up to it; but if the Lord sent me a teacher, then we could do this: you come together with her — I assure you I would be happier — and leave the Superior Adelaide in Piacenza.8 What do you say?

10. If you were in Piacenza we could do this: find two paid teachers for Ferrara and then take Apanasia without her sister and bring her here. This is something I confide to you. What do you say? This evening I shall write it to that person. But one would have to go to the Prefect and get two good ones; I wrote to them to look for one; they have not yet been to Cor., and I have written to Gargiolli.9

[-]10

1 Cf. L37.3.

2 leaving everything in good order. Sr. A. Francesca had written to her (19.2.73): «there is so much disorder that everything cannot be put right so quickly».

3 Don Tito Borgatta and the President Marco Montano were attentive to the Sisters.

4 The Mother's heart was always ready to help anyone in need and was not constrained by organizational schemes or difficulties.

5 Sr. A. V. = Sr. A. Tommasina Viterbo; she was 16; Sr. A. Francesca

in the L cited above had written to her: «I dare not leave Sr. A. Tommasina alone, there are certain faces! there is a man who instead of being in prison is here in the hospital, with a face that, to tell the truth, is frightening»!

6 Cf. L37.2; 40,11; 50,1.

7 In Rome she had dealings with the «Ladies of the Circle of St Monica».

8 Cf. L46, n. 4; L 50,1.

9 ...take — Apanasia — without her sister: Sr. A. Panasia was a teacher in Ferrara, where her sister Stella was also a boarder... I shall write it to that person (cf. L 2, n. 3): she wanted Fr Tornatore's opinion. ...get two good ones: have two good lay teachers recommended... have not yet been to Cor.: the abbreviation is unclear.

10 The greetings and signature are missing.

She hears that in Ovada they are making difficulties about her return to Piacenza. She should try to obtain consent to add two more religious and leave, because her presence is needed. The Mother will go to Foligno and then, at the Cardinal's invitation, to Perugia.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have received yours, in which I hear they are making difficulties about letting you come; now listen: meanwhile you can tell them that, since there is so much work and nothing will be charged to the Hospital, you are calling two religious to help you; and as soon as they agree, write to that Person, who will send them to you, because Sr. A. Adelaide will leave for Rome on the 4th or 5th.1

  2. On Monday I go to Foligno, where I shall stay until Saturday. I shall not write to you; you can address your letters to Rome, for I shall collect them on my return, since I certainly won't have a moment to breathe.2

  3. And moreover I shall have to go to Perugia; today I informed the Cardinal, as he required it of me.3

  4. I hope you will soon be able to return to Piacenza and at least call the other two nuns at once. You ask me to whom to leave the keys: to the Superior, Sr. A. Giacomina.

  5. If you persuaded the president and told him you are going, but

that at a word from him you would return, and the same to Don Tito, I think they will let you go. You should go to Piacenza on Saturday the 8th.

  1. You understand: so many postulants as there are and keep entering, and then the girls, the cleaning (le) and so many things; so relieve me of (in) worry, for the mere thought that she will be left alone pains me. And I would be very glad if you were there, because I want to know something about the linen; enough. Try to be as quick as you can.4

  2. You tell me about the pasta, and I say we must make do; buy the fine kind; as for bread, it will be better to make it at home, [there will be] more saving, and meanwhile you can buy a little flour. I think that is the right way. Quickly, hurry up, for you see there is need.

I'll stop, for I am as tired as a beast of burden.5 Goodbye. Give my regards to Don Tito, and believe me your

affectionate Mother

1 She has decided to send Sr. A. Adelaide to Rome and so gives her the appropriate instructions. On increasing the number of Sisters, cf. L49,6; 40,11.

2 On 6.3.73 Sr. A. Vincenza wrote to Sr. A. Francesca that she had left on the 4th «to open the Chapel and arrange the schools» and the Sisters, the tenants having vacated the house. Cf. Index IV.

3 Cf. L51.

4 The Mother gave good reasons for wanting her in Piacenza, but Sr. A. Francesca's presence was also indispensable in the hospital, and she could leave only on the 10th.

5 as tired as a beast of burden. Sr. A. Vincenza writes in the Memorie cited: they went to the new house, «which was completely empty, with only bare walls and a few iron beds the Mother had already sent from Rome». Everything still to be done!

■

She announces her imminent journey to Foligno and hopes to see him again.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. I gladly fulfil my duty of informing Your Most Reverend Eminence that next Monday, the 3rd of this month, I shall leave Rome on the 9 a.m. train for Foligno.

  2. Bless me, that I may have a good journey and have the good fortune to come and pay my respects to you again.1

At your feet, I remain Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

I Come to receive you = to pay my respects. She had first met him in Rome, and having heard about the Institute he had invited her to visit him in Perugia, «very much wishing the Mother to go and set up a foundation there for home nursing and for Schools» (Rapallino, Memorie cited).

Having received the letter, the Bishop invited her on 7.3.1873 to come to him.

She reports on enrolments at the School. She asks that the Prince her Consort recommend the approval of the Constitutions to Bishop Vitelleschi.

My Princess,

  1. A line in my own hand to give you good news of Your School: today more than 10 girls came to be admitted, all after Easter.1 Most of them are girls who attend the Municipal Schools. Others came yesterday after Your Excellency had left, but since they were from that Parish from which we are forbidden to accept pupils, I sent them away. On hearing this they said: «Very well, we shall send them to the Government Schools»;2 and I am quite certain that this work Your Excellency has done for the poor will be your consolation on earth and your joy in Heaven.

  2. Allow me to ask you a favour: that you have the Prince your most noble Consort recommend to Bishop Vitelleschi my great matter of the Constitutions, that is, Rules,3 for today our good, and all the good of God's Work, depends on Him, so that I may soon obtain everything. My Princess, this is a very great thorn for me.

  3. Sure that Your Excellency will obtain this favour for your most faithful servant, who never forgets the good already received, just as the favour she asks will never be forgotten.4 I hope in God to show you my gratitude in deeds rather than words.

I remain Your Illustrious Excellency's

Most humble Sr. Anna M. R. G.

1 after Easter, that is, after 15 April.

2 from that parish = it was not appropriate to accept pupils from other

Catholic schools. Here, however, the Mother wants to record the mothers' reply and determination.

3 The princess replied that her husband had spoken with Mgr Vitelleschi, who assured him of his prompt interest once he received the Constitutions «in full». Cf. AFSA, 72, RdP 29.

4 // good received, her active interest in the opening of the two houses in Rome: Tor de' Specchi and the Parrocchietta.

A Sister whom she had to transfer because the climate did not suit her will arrive in her community. She is to send Sr. A. Domenica to Rome and act prudently to avoid complaints from third parties.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. You will receive this from one of our Religious, whom I had to send away because the air does not agree with her; see whether she can get on well with you. I hope so, given your good manner. I hope it will go well; I warn you she has a very long tongue.2

  2. Now, my dear daughter, I'll confide something to you: I would like you to send me Sr. A. Domenica; you can let her go alone when a letter reaches you from Piacenza, because I need her for Rome; since she is not a teacher, I don't think they can say anything.3

  3. Neither where she is going nor where she comes from: silence; and if by misfortune she should meet that kind person,4 she is to give her no information: I have been called from Piacenza; and if she has a cough, let her say: to see whether my cough gets better. And after all, that's a fine thing — can one no longer place whom one wants? Anyway, I hope all will be well.

Goodbye, goodbye, dear; I am your

affectionate Mother Rosa

1 The date is inferred from the Mother's message to Sr. A. Adelaide (L54,2) of 5 March: Sr. A. Geroloma (Piralli) «leaves for Ferrara this morning... how much harm her tongue has done».

2 The traits described here match those in note 1.

3 Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini later became Superior of the House at the Parrocchietta. Prudence was needed so as not to hinder the transfer.

4 She refers to Countess Maria Anna Trotti.

She is to send three nursing Sisters to Foligno, and also dispatch the trunk with the linen and other articles. She should take care of herself, taking whatever she thinks good for her health.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I arrived here in Foligno yesterday and found two letters from you. Listen: I had written to that person to send me 3 nurses at once; for charity's sake, if Sr. A. Crocifissa (se) is ill, don't send her.1

  2. Send me religious who are healthy and without a tongue, because Sr. A. Gerolama leaves for Ferrara this morning, being unwell, and how much harm her tongue has done.2 For charity's sake send them at once.

  3. You should send to Rome 5 straw mattresses and some of those sheets I told you are mixed, having been brought by the postulants, so as not to spoil the wardrobe; likewise 12 pillowcases, also of the odd ones the postulants brought recently, 12 sheets, also 8 towels, one tablecloth; 12.3 Send me some heavy kitchen aprons and two woollen blankets; address it to Sr. A. Vincenza; send it by slow goods train, as it costs much less. Understood? By slow goods train.

  4. Send me the religious; try to buy them their

tickets to Florence from Piacenza, so they need not manage changes in Bologna.4

5. Today I am writing to Ferrara to see if I can take Sr. A. Domenica, for she would be very suitable for Rome;5 I'll stop.

My dear, for pity's sake take care of yourself, get rid of that cough, otherwise how can you come? It is a serious matter; I fear you may suffer. Try taking some lichen,6 in short whatever you think good. Goodbye, I am your

Affectionate Mother. Be cheerful: that is the best remedy you can have.

1 Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi.

2 Healthy and without a tongue. The spontaneous expression packs in a good deal. Healthy, because they would have to work hard; without a tongue, prudent and wise, because they would live among ordinary people, often curious. Cf. L53,l.

3 sheets... mixed, meaning not all of the same kind of cloth. One tablecloth, 12: she did not add what, perhaps napkins.

4 manage changes: the bustle of changing trains.

5 Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini.

6 Lichen, a lichen decoction to cure the cough.

As soon as she receives the telegram she is to leave at once and accompany the Sister assigned to Ferrara; in Bologna she will collect Sr. A. Domenica and take her to Rome. Meanwhile she is to send the trunk to Rome.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. How glad I am about your arm, that you are better, and also that Sr. A. Crocifissa is coming soon; for charity's sake send me these religious.1

  2. Listen: in Piacenza there is a small altar stone, but I don't remember where it was left, that is, where it is; if need be, without further ado, you can tell Don Gaetano to get it for you so that it may be placed here in this Chapel,2 and if the religious have already left, bring it yourself when you come, which will be soon.

  3. I hear all you tell me about Rocca. Poor unfortunate woman, let us pity her.3 As soon as you receive the telegram, come at once; I hope you have also received my letter telling you to send a trunk with linen, 12 of the postulants' sheets, pillowcases etc., which I won't repeat for lack of time. Instead of addressing it to Sr. A. Vincenza, address it thus: To the President of Tor de' Specchi, the Marchioness Galleffi;4 by slow goods train; and have prayers said. Don't put in anything that could cause trouble,5 no vermouth, rum or the like, for pity's sake, or you will displease me, because when it arrives there they will open it at the door.

  4. Be sure to send me the religious. You mention the Sister's shifts, that she has few: it doesn't matter, since in Rome the washing is done every week; forbid Sr. A. Angelica to cut cloth. I absolutely want Gaudenzi to collect the money first.6

  5. To send the religious to Ferrara, that is, the teacher, do this: when you pass through, take her to Bologna, and since the Superior Bucciotti will bring Sr. A. Domenica to Bologna to hand her over to you to take to Rome, she will take the teacher.7 Understood? Write and tell me if you have; then she will be a real help to you in Rome. Are you pleased?8 Enough for now, I am as tired as a beast of burden. Goodbye

your affectionate Mother Rosa G.

1 About your arm. Sr. A. Adelaide had an abscess in the armpit; the doctor had lanced it and she felt much relief. Sr. A. Crocifissa... these religious: cf. L 54,1.

2 Don Gaetano Bersani, a friend of Alessandro, M. Rosa's son; he put him up when he came to Piacenza and looked after him. He also did small administrative services for the Mother House. Sr. A. Francesca mentions him in her correspondence with M. Rosa.

3 Signora Marianna Rocca, wife of Count Stanislao Portapulia, was nursed by the Daughters of Saint Anne; unfortunate means deserving pity for her condition (she had long been ill) and for what she says. Adelaide had reported some of her opinions (L 4.3.73): «this is an Institute that makes martyrs of the young; they come in rosy and plump, and soon die, and other stories that would take me two days to write out».

4 telling you to send, cf. L 54,3. Galleffi, cf. L 38, n. 1.

5 that could cause trouble: anything that might cause problems.

6 Sr. A. Angelica Dematteis, the wardrobe keeper. She was untidy and rather careless in her office (cf. L Pezzoni, 28.2.'73 to M. Rosa). Gaudenzi, cf. L 46,5.

7 that is = more precisely the lay teacher. Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini.

8 Note the motherly tone and gentle expressions, showing full understanding for this beloved daughter, so tried and worn out by illness and ready in obedience to go and work in Rome.

She has received her two letters, agrees with her decisions and rejoices at her news. She regrets, however, the physical «labours» she and the Sisters take on. She should organize the night-watch rota well and see to the Sisters' food. The Mother will return to Rome next week for the commitments of the Work and the opening of the new house.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have received your letters; in the first you told me of the Sister who was not very good; I hear from the last one, received today, that she is better. In the second you asked about the timetable: yes, have the bell rung a quarter of an hour earlier, and if you need to, ring the small bells too.2

  2. Now you tell me about the President, and I am pleased, as I am that the two nurses are coming.

  3. I shall call the Superior Adelaide on Wednesday, but, my dear, I am very afraid she may fall ill in Rome. Enough; I am writing now to that person to tell me how she really is.3

  4. I am displeased with you because you overwork, and the others too. Certain heavy jobs you can have done by a daily woman.4

  5. You mentioned a postulant: accept her without waiting for my opinion; by now you are well instructed, so go ahead.

  6. Mind the night watch: I had said that with a bell connected to the Sisters' room they could all go to bed, as the Sisters do when there [are] no patients in danger of death; that little room you mentioned is a good idea, but the Sister must be changed every night, so the sheets must be changed and another go in.

  7. I can't wait for you to return to Piacenza, because I greatly fear something of the linen and everything may be spoiled in that house. In short, you understand; and then, with new postulants there, I tell you I am very worried.

  8. For pity's sake take care of yourself, for you see well that health is not to be gambled with. Watch out, shake up Giacomina,5 and for charity's sake let them never go out of the Hospital except to visit the sick and somewhere of great importance.

  9. I hope you have received mine about eating the fine pasta and making bread at home. The rest of what you wrote is fine.

  1. Now I tell you I am here in the midst of toil and haven't time even to pray, so I shall not write again from here, for next week I return to Rome.6

  2. Towards the end, Thursday or Wednesday, we shall be in our own house, but it lacks everything and we are looking around. Enough; I hope that here too good God will console us and send us what we need.7

Goodbye. Greet all the Sisters, who I hope now number 5; you will have put Pacifica in the kitchen.8 Goodbye, I am your

affectionate Mother Rosa

1 The original letter is dated 7 February, but it is certainly from 7 March, as the content clearly shows, in full agreement with the context.

2 The two letters she answers have not survived.

3 Wednesday: 12 March. Cf. L 49,9.

4 certain heavy jobs: general cleaning of all the rooms, reorganizing the kitchen, the linen room, etc. Sr. A. Francesca had written (19.2.73): «you cannot imagine the filth there is, and the linen is pitiful...».

5 Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi was certainly not of Sr. A. Francesca's mettle. Cf. L 40,4.

6 in the midst of toil. She too was working hard to set up the community in the new house in Foligno.

7 She refers to Rome, where at last they will be able to live in a house «of our own», that is, reserved for the Sisters (cf. L 38); but there too everything is lacking and God's help is awaited with filial trust.

8 Sr. A. Pacifica Bassi.

She asks her to send to Rome the receipt for the trunk she dispatched.

Dear daughter,

  1. I would like you to send me the receipt for the goods you dispatched; you can send it in the letter addressed to me in Rome, where, God willing, I shall be on Monday.2

  2. Tell the Sisters to pray for me, and see that you do what you promised me, to pray etc. Oh! I really need it; I add nothing more, you know.

Goodbye, a warm embrace in the heart of Jesus, and I am your

affectionate M. Rosa. Warm greetings to my dear daughters.

1 Addressee and date are missing. From the content and context it is clearly addressed to Sr. A. Adelaide: cf. L 55,3 and 56,3. The date is inferred from Sr. A. Adelaide's reply of 8.7.'73 announcing the dispatch.

2 She returned to Rome on Monday 17 March. Cf. L 64,1.

She will write to the Superior about what she asked. She urges her to be patient and to pray.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Just one line, because I am extremely busy and haven't a moment to breathe. I shall have the Superior written to, to let you stay with the others.2

  2. For the rest, be patient and you will see that this your very poor Mother will satisfy you in all you desire; meanwhile pray, for prayer is the key to the Lord's treasure. Courage and patience: everything is obtained. Goodbye, may the divine Lamb console you. I am your poor

M. Rosa

1 The addressee is not named. From tone, content and context it appears to be addressed to Colomba Grampini: cf. L 47,2 and the related note.

2 The Superior is Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti.

She should try to eat well and ask for nourishing broth. In the morning she should take fresh goat's milk.

My daughter,

  1. I hear all you tell me in the letter I received today.2 I tell you not to eat salty food, and I give you permission to say so whenever it doesn't suit you. Likewise tell them to make the broth nourishing.

  2. If in the morning you could take a little goat's milk warm as soon as it is milked — and if you could have donkey's milk, better still.

  3. Meanwhile have the goat brought to the door every morning at once and try it, but do everything very calmly; if Sr. A. Francesca is there, tell her; if not, do it yourself, for I want all this done; but don't waste time waiting for Sr. A. Francesca.3 Goodbye, for it is late.

I am your M. Rosa

1 The date is inferred by comparison with the correspondence of March 1873.

2 ...received today: that letter is dated 11 March 1873.

3 The Superior Francesca had returned from Ovada on the 10th but had left again for Genoa to collect a novice. Such is the news in Sr. A. Adelaide's letter mentioned in n. 2.

She is sorry about Alessandro's illness and asks that he be cared for. She herself is very unwell for various reasons. She should try to move Sr. A. Adelaide to a smaller room, as she needs to place the postulants she will bring with her.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have received your letters and hear that you have arrived in Piacenza.

  2. I am most grieved that Alessandro is ill; I would have liked you to see him.1 Well, I hope Don Gaetano has now gone to fetch him and taken him to his house.2 For pity's sake, look after him.

  3. I am so shaken I can barely hold the pen; very unwell, first from last night's fright,3 then I received 4 letters, all with a good dose of wormwood.

  4. Amid so many tribulations I fear for my mind, for I truly feel it is splitting; but patience. My God, what suffering!

  5. Listen: I think Sr. A. Adelaide sleeps in that big room with two other iron beds with curtains, and I would like to believe she has never lain in those. Well: you should gently persuade her [to] move to Buon Pastore's room, taking her bed there and put-

ting the chest of drawers there and a Sister to sleep, telling her I need two beds in that room well prepared, and that I wrote to you to have it whitewashed, the curtain washed and the beds put in order.4

  1. If she could be moved with her own mattress and straw mattress, leaving the iron bed there after a good scrub with lye,5 or else have it painted, because I shall bring postulants down, and you understand, they are young ladies and certainly cannot (ci) be put in that dormitory upstairs. So you see the whole time is needed to wash the curtains and have it whitewashed; it will take a month.6

  2. Listen: I know that on Saturday Eletta, the Superior of S. P. d'Arena, arrives; put her in the Father's bed and the others upstairs.7 Understood? For pity's sake don't let Sr. A. Adelaide be upset. See that she is well sheltered in that room; Sr. A. Agnese will sleep there; I don't think she can catch anything, being already elderly.8

  3. Tell her I want her to tell me whether she is happy, really happy. Shelter it well; first let her put there everything she likes, and keep it always closed; but she will be patient, for putting her with postulants, young ladies at that, who watch even one's breathing, she would feel too constrained and at night too embarrassed; but tell her to get well soon, and then she will come to Rome, where everyone is waiting for her.9

  4. Goodbye; I commend Gigino to you, and whatever you do for him I shall take as done to me; God will reward you.10

Send the girl Valle away without regard for human respect; and write about Albarelli.11

[your most affectionate Mother]

1 On her way back from Ovada she could have gone to Novi Ligure to visit Alessandro at boarding school there. The boy had let her know he had bad rheumatism in his right arm.

2 Don Gaetano. Cf. L 55, n. 2.

3 During the night some ill-wishers had set fire to the house door. Cf. Rapallino, Memorie cited, and Fiocchi I, p. 246.

4 to the room of Buon Pastore Dosi. This Sister had been transferred to the other house in Piacenza. Putting... to sleep. She explains further in paragraphs 7 and 8.

5 moved with her own mattress: move only her mattress to the other room, leaving the iron bed where it was, but disinfected and painted.

6 You see... month. Bear in mind it will take a month to do everything.

7 Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi was to sleep in the room once reserved for Fr Tornatore, and the Sisters arriving with her on the upper floor.

8 Sr. A. Agnese, the house nurse, could not catch Adelaide's illness.

9 She urges the greatest delicacy and every attention, so that she may not be in the least hurt nor her painful sufferings increased. Finally an exhortation and a hope: get well soon... she will come to Rome, everyone is waiting for her.

10 whatever you do... reward you. Words of strong human feeling, full of love and sorrow, of faith and a renewed offering of herself and her children to God.

11 Giuseppina Valle, one of the first girls taken in in 1867; the Albarelli sisters, Margherita and Silene, were withdrawn by their father the following June. (Cf. L of their father Roberto to Sr. A. Francesca, 27.6.1873, AFSA F24.5).

She gives news of Alessandro and asks her to speak to Sr. A. Vincenza about Signora Pisoni. She encloses a letter from a friend of hers. Sr. A. Vincenza is to tell the Princess of Viano that to serve the Pope she is ready for any sacrifice.

A.M.F. Dear daughter,

  1. I have just received a telegram that Alessandro is better and Don Gaetano has gone to fetch him.2 Listen: tell Sr. A. Vincenza to tell Signora Pisoni that I did not reply at once because I received the letter late; I don't know if it is still in time to tell her what she wanted, but I hope Saint Anne has done what her servant could not, having received the letter late;3 I shall tell her the reason in person; likewise Franceschina's, which I won't answer now, since I shall come on Monday; on the 6 o'clock train I shall be in Rome with Ninetta.4

  2. I am also sending you the letter from your friend, the niece of the Parish Priest of Nizza. In haste. Goodbye.

  3. I have received yesterday's letter telling me what the Princess of Viano wants; you can answer that to serve the Pope I would make any sacrifice, even of my very life, and that she may count on all the religious Daughters of Saint Anne and dispose of them as she pleases in every way, and that I shall send her the linen myself.6

  4. For that country house too I shall send her all the linen she wants; meanwhile tell her that on Monday I shall be

in Rome; she may tell Mgr Paca too, and the Princess may do as she thinks best and dispose of the Daughters of Saint Anne.7 Goodbye, see you soon

1 The addressee is missing in the original, but it is certainly Carlotta, as appears from the content and from the letters she wrote to the Mother together with Sr. A. Vincenza.

2 Cf. L 60,2.

Signora Celestina Pisoni, through Sr. A. Vincenza, had asked her advice on whether to keep the «candle shop» or not. (The Cereria Pisoni shop still exists in Corso Vittorio Emanuele, Rome).

4 Franceschina is Sr. A. Francesca Camisa; she does not write to her because she will return to Rome on Monday 17th with Ninetta (Caterina) Biagini, who wishes to join the FSA.

5 The niece of the Parish Priest Don Bisio, her friend, met in Nizza in January 1872.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have just received your telegram and see that Alessandro is in Piacenza. I beg you, my Francesca, give him nothing but inhalations and wool next to the skin. I hope it is nothing.2

  2. This morning too I had my fill of spasms, with another a few hours ago; enough, for the love of God everything is little.

affectionate Mother Rosa

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Just a line: you will hear what you are to take; I wrote to Sr. A. Eletta to get two goats if one is not enough, so that you have warm milk all day; try to take it warm when they milk it. About oranges I wrote: only a few, because they bring on fever.2

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

your affectionate Mother Rosa

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Rest assured that when I return I shall stop at your house and stay a good while, but unfortunately for now I must be here, as long as God wills. affectionate Mother Rosa

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Father Fava, whom she consulted, thinks the Rules should be entirely rewritten. Fearing their spirit may be changed, she asks that two more «Servants of God» be joined to him for the drafting and that they hear her, to safeguard the spirit. She asks him to reinstate Fr Tornatore in the direction of the Mother House.

Most Reverend Excellency,

  1. Allow me to tell you in writing what I could not express in person. Two days ago I spoke with the Rev. Father Fava, and he told me that he has done nothing yet about the Rules, that they must be rewritten, and that it will take another five or six months. These words were so many dagger thrusts to me; two months in Rome and I have achieved nothing!2

  2. My Lord, I beg you to grant my petitions, namely to join two other Servants of God to Father Fava, and that they have the kindness and charity to hear me, because if he gives the Rules a new spirit, it would no longer be our Institute and would bring in another spirit.

  3. If the Church required me to observe them, I would obediently bow my head and try to study this new spirit.3

  4. In all frankness I confess to you a strong, strong temptation of mine: to lay everything down, as I can no longer bear such prolonged anguish.

  5. In Piacenza there is a house with 140 people, postulants and religious, and I have been away from it for two months. The one who helped me, as you well know, is no longer allowed to go there. He alone could help me. The Bishop is unwell, the Vicar almost senile.4

  6. If Your Most Reverend Excellency would deign to summon this Religious and give him whatever obediences and commands you

think fit and then reinstate him,5 I could be freer to attend to the other houses and answer new calls,6 and meanwhile I would know that good Daughters of Saint Anne are being formed in that Mother House; and there are a thousand temporal matters to arrange that cannot be handled by letter.

7. Tomorrow I shall surely be at your feet with a most learned churchman,7 whom I consult, as I now place myself there to implore your apostolic blessing, while I remain with veneration Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. For charity's sake, I beg you to see that the girls in their refectory do not throw food away, as they do now and always have done, being naughty to excess. Listen: the first who has polenta, soup or bread left over and throws it under the table, send her away without fail; I don't want a single crumb on the floor. Leaving some on the plate means nothing, but on the floor, no.2

  2. Oh, you know how many times I told these wretched girls they will have to learn the value of what they waste!3 I also wrote the rest to that person, so that this may be remedied.4

5. Here money goes like the wind; I still have some of my own, but I assure you everything costs money. I am in a hurry; your

affectionate Mother Rosa

She gives detailed explanations and instructions on refitting the postulancy and other cleaning work in the house. She should ask the Father to copy out the Rules for the mistress of postulants and of novices.

A.M.F.

My daughter

  1. I am answering yours straight away; well done — after two letters you answer one: so I am always in credit!

  2. So, to the basin: let it be 6 to 7 spans long with 3 taps; buy it at once; have [another] smaller one (la) fitted with two taps, and that one for the kitchen; yes, have it bought at once, God will pay for everything. Have it set between the windows, like the one in the lamp room we already spoke of.2

  3. You are right to put the stove in our dormitory; I would put it in the middle with an iron pipe overhead running to where you say, where the chest of drawers was; that way the tables, being long, would not be in the way, and it would not give off the heat one wants. The refectory is fine as you said.

  4. Listen, leave the two rooms; instead we'll do this: the girls' refectory will serve as the postulants' recreation room, and I would have the girls' kitchen knocked through and put in good order, with two chests of drawers and chairs, nicely arranged, the door with clean glass; everything well whitewashed, and the privy too. What do you think? Light green on the door, and on the gratings.3

  5. Do you know what we'll do? We'll have all the big shutters in the corridor painted; you know how bad they look. If it could be done, see whether it would take about 100 F.;4 I would be very pleased.

  6. Do you know, my Vincenza, that via Falconara it costs much less? Rome to Falconara is 21.70 F.; what do you think? Losing 73 F. from Rome to Piacenza! It's better that way. How distressing! (You) cannot imagine what it is to see money always being spent and no large providence ever coming.5

  7. For the sick, don't do anything, because they cost too much.6 You see we have so many expenses that for now it's not possible. Listen: make the girls' refectory where the looms are, I mean the room with the altar, but with everything removed and locked in the room before the looms, always kept locked. Beyond the alcove, all round, all the benches and tables, and part of it will serve for the postulants, enlarging the refectory. Listen: find three good heavy curtains, hang one long at the alcove and the other two small ones at the sides, so nothing will be seen.7 What do you think? One still to be made, that is Tuzzi's new striped bedspread, and I know there are others in the linen room.8 I think it will look well whitewashed.

  8. What do you say? I'm driving you mad, aren't I? Just let me give orders! Be patient! Still, it's true these things can be done without the work on the rooms, which we won't speak of again.9 Do everything quickly, then you will come and fetch me; but first appoint the mistress of postulants and the mistress of novices, clothing two or three, and then put them in the novitiate.

  9. Tell that person to make a good copy of the Rules for the mistress of postulants, removing the dialogue form. They will serve Sr. A. Giovanna for the postulants [and] Sr. A. Cecilia for the novices. All right? So, courage!10

10. Write and tell me whether our room is ready, and yours. Now one more thing. Have tulle put on the beds in the girls' dormitory, which I hope will be locked; at least on the four curtain rods, and have them screwed onto the rods themselves, because I shall need them — I'll tell you later — but they must always stay locked there and no one use them.11 Courage, God will see to everything, I hope.

  1. The girl the Municipality sent you — did they also send the 50 F. as they always do? If not, have them sent. Dear Vincenza, I am not short of crosses, but this week they are doubling on every side.

  2. How many postulants have you? Goodbye; I hope this letter finds you in Piacenza. You did well to have the girls go to confession, so they will make their Easter duty.12

Goodbye, my dear. Rest assured you won't lose your place, because no one does what you used to do; I do everything myself, everything. Goodbye, dear daughter; believe me yours on earth and in heaven

[Mother Rosa]

1 Sr. A. Vincenza had gone to Piacenza in early April.

2 Practical, detailed advice for preparing the postulancy rooms. A good deal of money will be needed, but the Mother has faith in providence and says so with certainty: God will pay for everything.

3 The advice is precise, as if she were on the spot with nothing else to do.

4 about F.: some hundred francs.

5 via Falconara: she means that taking the Rome–Falconara–Piacenza line costs less.

6 For the sick (= for the infirmary) do no work, because it costs too much. She had given the same advice to Sr. A. Francesca.

7 ...all'arcova: alcove.

8 She probably means adapting as curtains the striped bedspread of Vittoria Tuzzi (a postulant) and others in the linen room.

9 These things can be done without too much expense, but not the work on the rooms, of which no more is to be said.

10 Fr Tornatore was to copy the Rules (a regulation) for the Mistress of Postulants, Sr. A. Giovanna Bixio, and for the Mistress of Novices, Sr. A. Cecilia Tortini.

// Fr Fava has been unable to deal with the Constitutions. Cardinal Vannicelli has returned them to her, and she hands them over so that he may officially entrust them to two Consultors for the urgent revision, since she has so many religious to form in the spirit of the Constitutions. She wishes the Consultors to hear her regarding any observations.

Most Reverend Excellency,

  1. I am sending you the latest Constitutions, which I had given to Father Fava and which this most pious Rev. Father has not yet been able to deal with.1

  2. Cardinal Vannicelli, seeing that this matter would drag on too long, gave them back to me, and I place them in Your Rev.de hands, that Your Most Reverend Excellency may deign to refer them to one or two consultors with an official note, so that the much-desired praise may soon be obtained.2

  3. Most Reverend Excellency, it is hard to believe how much distress this matter causes me, having so many religious to instruct in this spirit and nothing, neither printed nor handwritten; I ask it of you for pity's sake. Your Most Reverend Excellency can do everything.3

  4. I would also wish these Consultors to have the charity to hear me, should there be any observation to make.4

  5. I hope to obtain everything, and when I return from Mgr Negrotto's country estate, where I am going after lunch to open a school,5 I shall come to Your Most Reverend Excellency for your instructions and to receive some good news, of which I have no doubt, having always found in you a charitable Father.

Please grant me your Apostolic blessing, while I remain with the greatest veneration Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 The latest Constitutions, that is, those she composed in Ferrara. They had not been approved, and it had been decided to have them drawn up by Fr Leonardo Fava SJ. Cf. Lettere 2, p. 15.

2 // Card. Vannicelli, the Protector of the Institute. The desired praise: the approval.

3 «...how much distress... to instruct». She is pressed at heart by the longing to form the Sisters in the spirit of the Institute. She has every reason to be anxious: she is away from Piacenza opening new houses, and Fr Tornatore is no longer allowed to act as formator as in the past.

4 to hear me. She had very clear ideas about the spirit that should inform the Constitutions and defended their genuineness: cf. Lettere 2, L 329 and in this Vol. L 68.

)

She has delivered the Rules to Mgr Vitelleschi and asks for his fatherly and authoritative support with him.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. Today I delivered the Rules to Monsignor Vitelleschi, begging him to take them up, and so that this may happen1 I turn to Your Most Reverend Eminence, who has always been a Father to me, to say just one word to this Bishop, and that is enough to obtain everything.

  2. Forgive your very little daughter, who, having no other Father than Your Most Reverend Eminence, keeps coming to trouble you.

Please grant your Apostolic blessing to my two children,2 and to her who remains with the greatest veneration Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 Cf. the previous L.

2 Carlotta and Alessandro.

Most Illustrious Inspector,

1. The undersigned, wishing to devote her Work to the benefit and advantage of poor girls, asks the Royal Inspector to grant permission to open a free girls' School outside Porta S. Pancrazio, called the Parrocchietta.2 The undersigned encloses the necessary documents.

Confident of a favourable reply, she remains with the highest and deepest esteem Your Illustrious Lordship's

Most humble N.N.

She has received her letter. Yes, she may accept the postulants, but she is to send them to Piacenza at once.

[My daughter]

1. I received your letter yesterday. I was very ill and could not hold the pen; today, poorly. So yes, accept the postulants, both the old one and the other, but I want them to leave for Piacenza at once.2 Keep 1000 F., and they will take the rest with them, because clothings cost a great deal. So let them leave for Piacenza at once. Have prayers said, because I am very ill and cannot go on; your

affectionate Mother Rosa

1 The date is inferred from that of the addressee's letter, 5 April, which the Mother is answering.

She was glad to hear of the good journey. She will return to Rome when summoned by telegram. She is to choose two Sisters: one to bring with her, the other to leave in Foligno. The Mother has been to Mgr Vitelleschi and to the Schools Inspector.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I received your telegram and was glad to hear of the good journey and also of the hope that they will do everything; I am at Tor de' Specchi and have just come back from V. My God, patience! «Tradri», Carlotta says [to] Mgr Mariano; what a world! There's not a clean finger's breadth left.2

  2. You will leave when you receive a telegram from me. Bring with you someone who can teach a little, and if there is no one else take Sr. A. Palmira, but make sure she can at least teach from the wall charts; that's enough.3

  4. I am tired; this morning I also went to the Inspector and obtained everything; he was a lamb, all goodness.5 I took him the good-conduct certificates. Enough; now all is well.

Give my regards to the Superior and Sr. A. Adelaide,7 and believe me

your affectionate Mother

2 Glad to hear of the good journey... everything. Sr. A. Vincenza had gone to Genoa on business concerning the Ricchini case. I have just come back from Vitelleschi, the Secretary of the S. Vincenza on 11 April: «We went to Vitelleschi. What a grouch! He gave her no satisfaction at all!».

She has received her letter enclosing one for her brother-in-law Cardinal Barnabò. She went to him and also spoke of the Foligno house and its straits, but lacked the courage to ask for a subsidy. She begs her to intercede.

Dearest Marchioness,

  1. I received your esteemed letter enclosing one for Cardinal Barnabò, your brother-in-law;1 I would have liked to deliver it in person and at the same time receive His Eminence's Apostolic blessing, but my poor health prevented me, and only on Saturday did I have that good fortune.

  2. On returning home I would have liked to send you these two poor lines and tell you how charitably I was received while I commended my business to him, so that I was overwhelmed by so much kindness; but my headache returned and did not leave me until late yesterday, so I had to put off replying until today.

  3. I spoke at length with this Most Eminent Prince about Foligno and told him of our straits and the lack of alms, but I did not have the courage to ask him for a subsidy for it.2 As I came out I could not help exclaiming: «My God! how badly this donkey of yours serves you; have pity on me!».

  4. My Marchioness, you see how wretched and abject I am; I would beg Your Excellency to let the Cardinal know that I shall return and that my purpose will be to ask him for alms for the house

p

of Foligno; forgive me and also have pity on this your servant, who is incapable of serving well the supreme Master.3

5. I long to meet you and to tell you in person what thankfulness and gratitude dictate, while I remain in the Heart of Jesus your most faithful

Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

1 The Marchioness had sent her a letter of recommendation dated 1.4.73 for her brother-in-law Cardinal Alessandro, Prefect of Propaganda Fide. The Mother was able to go to him only on 5 April.

2 The noble Barnabò family came from Foligno. The Mother had lacked the courage to ask in person for a subsidy and regrets it; it had happened to her before. Cf. Lettere 2, L 2, n. 3 and L 275,4.

3 Expressions of candid sincerity and humility.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have a letter from Ferrara: the examinations have been postponed, so I hope you will come before I have to leave; tell mamma.1 The Prefect has not yet sent me the letter; prepare this one ready for me, so that as soon as I receive it I can have it posted at once.2

  2. Listen, before I forget: on your way back I want you to call on that lady in Pontedecimo and (e) ask her for a photograph of Rosa, and see how she is, and tell her I need to speak to her; tell her to pray that God may send me a little providence.3

  3. Be kind to the Vernengo sisters, I beg you; shower them with good, charitable words.4

  4. Yesterday I had prepared this letter to enclose with the Prefect's, but he has not sent it today either; I am writing to you lying down; don't be alarmed, for today I am a little better.5 The fever has almost gone. Come as quickly as you can; in appointing Sr. A. Eletta, say it is provisional until

the Superior returns, since she is at S. P. d'Arena as teacher and so also takes the Superior's place. If I can, I shall write two lines to be read aloud, but just now I really cannot.6

She is to act judiciously in dismissing the surplus girls. She is very sorry about her poor health. She explains her thinking about the sick Sisters: they should be moved to the House in Via della Morte, better equipped for them than the Mother House. She should put everything in order and be calm and at peace; perhaps the Mother will call her to Rome for a while. Prayers are to be said for Marchioness Cavalletti.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Today I received your letter together with one from Sr. A. Vincenza, to whom I am not writing, because by the time this reaches you she will already be on her way to Rome. I hope that person has also received my letter and explained to you what I wanted.2

  2. Now I hear from yours that you are sending girls away. Do it judiciously, I beg you, only where they don't pay and it is impossible to keep them, since there are so many.3

  3. My Francesca, you cannot imagine how sorry I was to read that you too are unwell; for charity's sake, daughter, look after yourself; vomiting ruins the stomach, and then, you see, you have Sr. A. Adelaide's example before you; they are so many dagger thrusts in my breast.

If you truly love me, look after yourselves and keep well; the Lord's work needs strong, healthy people.4

  1. I hope you understood the Superior Eletta's letter properly — or rather, I'm wrong, you didn't. I meant that you should not only leave Sr. A. del Buon Pastore, Sr. A. Veronica and all the chronic patients at the Morte,5 but also send there all the others you have in the house, because there they have more facilities for devotion, such as Holy Communion every day — they can receive it before Mass — and the infirmary [is] better in every way, whereas in your house [where] the infirmary is inconvenient, you would need the Church upstairs and a kitchen, while there they have everything.6

  2. I hear about Sr. A. Caterina; we should write to her mother saying her native air would do her good, see what she says, and then be patient; Saint Anne will see to it.7 If she sends us sick Sisters, she will send us the means. Let us trust in good God, and we shall have everything.

  3. You tell me nothing about whether Don Gaetano has paid. Who has the lottery money?8 Put everything in order, and when there are no more sick Sisters I shall arrange things so that you can come here for a while.

  4. Calm yourself, for peace of soul joined to bodily calm, with perfect resignation to God's will in everything, does our poor humanity a great deal of good. What is gained by fuming?   5. Carlottina badly needs a black dress; you can make it of wool muslin, and when the other Sisters come, or you with them, bring it.

  6. I can't understand how, of so many postulants who wanted to come, none come any more.

10. Every day I want the Hail Marys I say at noon to be for Marchioness Cavalletti, our great benefactress,10 who is in poor health and also has a bad eye complaint. The Saint must cure her; pray that she may soon be well.

visitors and also had a great deal of writing.

I am yours; the Lord bless you.

She is not to worry if the Mother does not write; she is not at all displeased with her, and her letters are a consolation. Courage, and always be cheerful.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. For pity's sake, my dear daughter, don't be anxious1 because I don't write, as if my silence meant I were displeased with your conduct — no, no; on the contrary, I am very pleased, and your letters are dear to me, especially when I hear such good news of providence.

  2. For charity's sake look after your health and think of getting better2 so as to work and pray; and I tell you in secret that if you are well you can put together a nice little purse; one day you too will come to see the Holy Father.

  3. So be cheerful, keep writing to me; and as for the penances you give, you do well; carry on.3

  4. If I don't write it is because I am immensely busy and really cannot. I write to no one — to no religious, that is. Greet everyone; I am your

Affectionate Mother Rosa

1 In her letter of 18 April Sr. A. Santina said she was worried by the Mother's silence.

2 The Sister had also told her of her physical sufferings and the remedies she was taking.

3 as for the penances, corrections given to the Sisters for external breaches of the Rule.

She asks permission to reserve the Blessed Sacrament in the little Chapel. She begs him to order Fr Tornatore to resume responsibility at least for the two houses in Piacenza, to relieve her of serious financial worries.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. The last time I was at your feet I forgot to ask whether in this little chapel we may use the permission we have to reserve the Most Holy Sacrament.2

  2. Meanwhile I take this opportunity to tell you of a great affliction of mine and ask your advice. The Superior of the main house in Piacenza writes that she is in need. Your Most Reverend Eminence knows well that there must be between one hundred and fifty and two hundred people in that house; we have another in the same city with a school that does great good, with 170 boys; it has been going very well for four years, and these are poor boys who used to play in the streets; instead they come to learn Christian doctrine and become good.

  3. After they removed Mr Tornatore from me — who, as confessor to all the nobility there, provided me with plentiful alms — this year I did all I could to keep this house going as it was.3

  4. The houses of Saint Anne now number twelve, all of which worry me, and the one in Piacenza more than all the others.4

  5. If Your Most Reverend Eminence would summon this Priest and, giving him orders and obediences, then allow him at least to look af-

ter those two houses in Piacenza, even leaving in force my prohibition from confessing to him and consulting him on spiritual matters; for a year now my director has been Jesus, and I am very content with this direction; I confess to anyone and am perfectly at peace.

6. The chapel would open tomorrow, provided Your Most Reverend Eminence gives consent. Please grant me the apostolic blessing, while I remain Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Humble Obl. Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

1 The draft (AFSA, 18 M1VP, p. 93) lacks addressee and date, which can however be inferred from the content.

2 use the permission we have: On 22.1.1866 Mother Rosa had obtained from Pius IX a rescript allowing her to erect a private oratory in the Houses the Institute would open, and other faculties including that of reserving the Blessed Sacrament (AFSA, SS. FI, 81). The faculties granted by Pius IX were, however, subject to the concessions of the «respective Bishops and Ordinaries». Little Chapel. It is not known in which of the four houses opened in Rome; perhaps Tor de' Specchi, the first House opened in Rome.

3 The work had continued to function normally despite the loss of support.

4 The houses are twelve, in order of opening: Mother House, Sampierdarena, Piacenza (Boys' School and Infirmary), Genoa, Ferrara, Nizza Monferrato, Ovada, Foligno, Rome (four).

She explains what linen to bring. For her coming to Rome she should proceed as follows: keep everything in order and leave as soon as she receives the telegram; but if Fr Santi is visiting the house, she is not to move until he has gone. Some advice about the girls.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I am answering yours, received a few hours ago, in which you tell me you have received mine and all the tickets etc.. You ask which tablecloths to bring: only two of ours, you know, from our refectory, the fringed ones, but not too long, just two; as for napkins, you can bring 4 cotton ones of the arengo(?) cotton kind, and the others from our refectory; towels, just a few, 6. Sheets as I told you.

  2. I didn't understand at all where that person is; I thought in Cremona... enough.2 Listen: today I had a dog's day over that person's affairs; how many enemies he has! I thought I would burst with grief, my God!3

  3. You ask what to do about Father Santi. If he has not yet come, lock up and off you go; come anyway; leave instructions with Buon Pastore, and what the portress is to say; if they are questioned, silence; and if he asks how many nuns we are, a large number; for charity's sake, do you understand me?4

  4. Have more postulants arrived? For charity's sake, don't give Buon Pastore the sheets from the linen room; keep them apart.5 I think your room would be better if your bed too had curtains; see whether you can arrange it.

  5. I hear about the girls; all is well, except the Cesena girls: remember their mother is wicked and would lead them into sin the moment she had them in her power, for charity's sake! Giuseppa Valle yes, but the two Cesena girls must be kept, with patience; likewise the Angel of Paradise.6 Warn Scopesi that she can no longer be kept; but don't send her away, if it can be avoided. «My God! send providence, and then we won't send them away».7

  6. So, have you understood? In any case, as soon as you get a telegram, come. If the telegram comes while you are busy with Father Santi, wait before coming; you all wait, and when Father Santi has gone you will all come together. Have you understood me?

  7. Why do you tell me you don't do all the washing? I think it would be good to do all of it, so you can still see how things are going; don't worry if you can't.

  8. See that Gazzola goes to the country.8 Everything else in person. Goodbye. You will have understood about Father Santi: if he is with you when the telegram arrives, wait until he leaves, then come.

Goodbye. In haste and standing up, I am your

Affectionate Mother. Bring two metres more of scotto besides what is needed for the clothing.9

1 The date is incomplete, but it is certainly April 1873.

2 Fr Tornatore.

3 She had evidently asked some Prelate that he be reinstated at least as director of the two Houses in Piacenza (cf. L 89, 3,5) and had discovered such hostility towards him that it caused her great suffering.

4 Fr Santi (cf. L 11, n. 3) was to visit the Mother House again. Lock up refers to cupboards and rooms. Note the precise instructions: she leaves Sr. A. Del Buon Pastore Dosi in charge of the house, explains how the portress is to answer any questions about the Superior's absence, and suggests explaining to the others how to behave and answer.

5 This Sister was ill.

6 Sr. A. Francesca was reducing the number of girls. The Mother alerts her about some of them. The Angel of Paradise is surely a very good little girl.

7 Adele Scopesi contributed to her daughter's keep. She was to be warned to pay, but the girl was not to be sent away. The Mother ends these painful remarks with an invocation to God and an urgent plea: send providence, and the doors of the house will not open to send them away.

8 For Maria Gazzola, one of the first to enter, she was to do her best to send her to the country for a while.

9 Two metres of scotto beyond what is needed for the clothing.

She sends him a letter from Mgr Mariano and, declaring herself resigned to God's will, begs him to help her in her troubles.

Most Reverend Father,

  1. Knowing how much you care for our good, I send you a letter I have just received from Monsignor Mariano; I hope it will be read only by Your Paternity.2

  2. This poor daughter of yours, who has no one else to whom she can unburden herself amid so many tribulations,3 tells you too that she is wholly resigned to God's will.

  3. My Father, my troubles are countless. Ah! for pity's sake help me, as you have already done so often, and one day I hope to tell you some of them.

Bless me and believe me always Your Reverence's

Most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 This letter falls within the chronological limits of Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist's letter of 23 April 1873.

2 On behalf of the Cardinal Protector Luigi Vannicelli, he informed her that Don Angelo Pacchino had sent him «a defamatory libel» against her and Fr Tornatore and that the Cardinal had written a long letter to Mgr Magnasco, Archbishop of Genoa, so that he might use his authority, if possible, to stop so much scandal and bitterness for the Mother (AFSA, VW1-83).

3 The Father replied on 27 April with a fine, consoling letter: «you must not be distressed», he said among other things, «but leave it to the Advocate. The Lord will defend the innocent and the poor» (ibid.).

She encloses a letter for the confessor. She has received a printed sheet from Don A. Ricchini.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received yours and hear of the good harmony in the House.2 I enclose two lines for the Confessor; give them to him at once.3

  2. Don Ricchini sent me a sheet (illegible word) with oaths in it, or rather about oaths; what an eccentric! let him be; it amuses him a little, since meanwhile he has nothing to do.4

  3. Tell the nurses to pray that I may obtain my grace. Give me news of mamma.5 Goodbye

your affectionate M.

1 The letter she answers is dated 27 April '73.

2 The community was serene and at peace.

3 The Confessor, recently appointed through Don Accinelli's intervention with the Archbishop, is Don Borgotto. Cf. Accinelli's L of 18 and 22 April.

4 Cf. L91, n. 2.

5 The grace she desired: approval of the Constitutions. Sr. A. Santina was on excellent terms with Signora Adelaide and often visited her.

She wishes to know whether he can grant her a brief audience.

Most Reverend Father,

  1. A thousand apologies if I trouble you again with my writing; being unable to help it, I must turn to the one who is a Father to me. I have just received your esteemed letter and find no word about the Parish Priest of the Fornaci.1

  2. Through the bearer of this note I should like to know whether you could hear me tomorrow for just a moment. If I am a nuisance, please forgive me.

  3. I have placed everything in God's hands and no longer care about anything. I want God's will alone, my Father, and in it I wish to die. Bless this your very poor daughter, who remains with the greatest veneration Your Reverence's

Most humble Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 She turned to him not only about the Rules but also for advice on the Rome houses. Another work had recently begun in Via delle Fornaci, within the parish of «S. Maria delle Fornaci».

She has received her letter and reassures her; she will not write at length, being very busy: she has opened four houses in a short time. She urges the greatest prudence, given the presence in the house of Signora Colomba and the lay teachers.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Yesterday evening I received your very sorrowful letter about yourself, since you took to heart the letter the Superior here wrote to you.2

  2. Listen: I grant you weren't thinking about what you said, and that your remark about the number of Sisters...; but if the letter had fallen into other hands, and you, not having been warned, had said this to outsiders, it would certainly have harmed the cause; enough, let it be over now, for I am writing in great haste.3

  3. My work has reached its peak — imagine! four houses have been opened in so short a time.4

  4. Now I'll tell you something I want you to do. Give Signora Colomba a room and then let her do as she pleases; only you must forbid her to come to your offices or to talk with the Sisters, and the Sisters and postulants must not let her hear anything at all, because I want her to know nothing, nothing, because...5

  5. Mind you never let yourself be heard saying anything to the Sisters, and they must never be heard asking you anything, nothing, I beg you. Only you should talk with her and,

when you go out, it will be good to take her with you so that she gets out a little and has some air.6

  1. She asks always to confess to this extraordinary confessor and would like to go to the church where he is; well, agree to it. Have her accompanied by Sr. A. Cecilia and the other, Sr. A. Ignazia, of course when it does not disturb the community and on a day convenient to you.7

  2. Then, about the outside teacher: I am writing to Colomba now so that she is not upset, because this teacher has certain books and says she does not believe in the Saints, that is, that the Lord admits no advocates; what a head, my God!8 Be patient, but for charity's sake make sure no one knows these things; I want you not (?) to be discreet. Alas! if this false talk, spoken and seen by this fanatical head, got about, how much harm it would do! Don't confide in her at all. And let the teacher have little or nothing to do with our religious and teachers, especially the young ones.9

Goodbye, I am tired

your affectionate M.

God bless all that community and give it peace...

P.S. Tell the teacher in confidence not to give her books to the religious or [to] others; all in silence.10

1 The date is inferred from Sr. A. P. Bucciotti's correspondence, especially her letters of 1 and 6 May 1873.

2 Being very busy, the Mother had had Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi, Superior of the Tor de' Specchi house, write to her.

3 On hearing that so many houses were opening she had written to the Mother: «there are more houses than religious». Sr. A. Eletta had pointed out how inappropriate this remark was. (Cf. L 27.4.73, AFSA, F35.2).

4 Houses opened in Rome in April 1873: Tor de' Specchi, the Parrocchietta, the Fornaci, Trastevere (Piazza S. Agata, 1).

5 Signora Colomba Grampini (cf. L 47, 2). She advises how to treat her, since she is not a postulant but a guest; so everyone in the house must be very prudent.

6 When you go out, it is good to take her with you.

7 Sr. A. Cecilia Tortini and Ignazia Losi, both experienced Sisters.

8 The «good» Signora Colomba was scandalized by the lay teacher's ideas.

9 I want you not (to speak of it), to be discreet. She evidently omitted the words speak of it; Have little... young ones. The Mother feared the Sisters and the other young teachers might be influenced by the teacher's unorthodox ideas.

10 Probably books not approved by the Church.

She points out that, as regards the advice she asks about the School, it is best to keep to what Don Bernardino has told her.

A.M.F.

Daughter,

  1. I have received your registered letter asking my opinion on what to do about the School, as that holy man Don Bernardino tells you. Oh! the advice of that excellent Priest is far too wise to be refuted by a wretched Servant of the Lord incapable of giving the slightest advice.2

  2. So hold firmly to whatever you receive from this Priest, and you will always be glad of it.

  3. Many greetings to Signora Biagini3 and to Don Bernardino; I commend myself to his prayers and to those of the Father Guardian,4 while I remain

Your most humble and devoted Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 The autograph letter lacks addressee and date; both are inferred from the content and the sequence of events. Maria Grampini, a teacher, was keen for the work to succeed.
